title: No Vibes Allowed: Solving Hard Problems in Complex Codebases – Dex Horthy, HumanLayer

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is context engineering for coding agents—intentional compaction, context window management, sub-agents for context control, and the Research-Plan-Implement workflow. The demonstrations and techniques center on coding agents operating in complex brownfield codebases like BAML's Rust codebase and Parquet Java. The techniques address operating AI coding agents in production codebases and adapting team workflows around them. Requires familiarity with LLM context windows, coding agents, and brownfield codebase challenges but is accessible to practitioners. This is a conference talk delivered at AI Engineer 2025. summary: Dex Horthy opens by referencing a Stanford study surveying 100,000 developers showing AI coding tools cause excessive rework and churn, especially in brownfield codebases, while working well for greenfield projects. He frames context engineering as the solution to getting the most out of today's models. The talk introduces 'intentional compaction'—compressing an existing context window into a tagged markdown file so a new agent can start immediately without re-searching. He explains what consumes context: file lookups, code flow understanding, edits, test/build output, and noisy MCP JSON dumps. The 'dumb zone' concept begins around 40% of the context window, where diminishing returns set in. Sub-agents should be used for context control, not anthropomorphized roles. The Research-Plan-Implement workflow structures context management across three phases. He demonstrates on a 300k LOC Rust codebase (BAML), where a oneshot fix PR was accepted by the CTO, and 35,000 lines were shipped in 7 hours. He then critiques 'spec-driven dev' as suffering from semantic diffusion—Martin Fowler's observation that good terms become useless when they mean too many things to different people. For agent onboarding, he recommends progressive disclosure: placing context files at each level of the repo hierarchy so agents pull in only relevant context, preserving smart zone capacity. He warns that internal docs decay and contain 'lies,' preferring on-demand compressed context built from code truth. Mental alignment is the real purpose of code review—keeping the team on the same page about how the codebase is changing. Plans should include actual code snippets for leverage and reliability. He emphasizes that human review of research and plans is the highest-leverage activity: a bad research line can send the model in the wrong direction, and a bad plan line could be a hundred bad lines of code. The amount of context engineering needed scales with problem complexity—simple changes need less, hard problems need more. He predicts coding agents will be commoditized, and the real challenge is adapting team workflows and culture. A rift is growing: staff engineers don't adopt AI because it doesn't make them faster, mid-levels use it and produce slop, and seniors resent cleaning it up. Cultural change must come from the top. He concludes: 'Do not outsource the thinking—AI can only amplify the thinking you have done or the lack of thinking you have done.'
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Frequent intentional compaction—compressing context into markdown files and restarting fresh agents—keeps agents in the 'smart zone' and dramatically improves results in complex codebases.
The 'dumb zone' begins around 40% of the context window; too many MCPs push all work into this zone, degrading output quality.
Sub-agents exist to control context, not to anthropomorphize roles; they fork out expensive reading/searching and return concise summaries to parent agents.
The Research-Plan-Implement workflow structures context management across three phases, keeping context small and explicit at each step.
Spec-driven dev has suffered semantic diffusion—the term now means too many things to too many people and has become useless.
Agent onboarding via progressive disclosure places context files at each repo level so agents pull only relevant context, preserving smart zone capacity.
Mental alignment is the real purpose of code review; plan review lets technical leaders maintain understanding of system evolution without reading every line of code.
Human review of research and plans is the highest-leverage activity: a bad research line can derail the entire effort, and a bad plan line could become a hundred bad lines of code.
The amount of context engineering needed scales with problem complexity—simple changes need less, hard problems need more; finding the sweet spot takes reps.
Cultural change must come from the top: a rift is growing where staff engineers avoid AI, mid-levels produce slop, and seniors resent cleanup; technical leaders should pick one tool and get reps.

sections.title: Intro: Stanford Study and the Slop Problem
sections.summary: Dex references the Stanford study surveying 100,000 developers showing AI coding tools cause excessive rework and churn in brownfield codebases while working well for greenfield projects. He frames the problem as context engineering: how to get the most out of today's models.

sections.title: Context Engineering and Intentional Compaction
sections.summary: Introduces intentional compaction—compressing an existing context window into a markdown file that a new agent can use to start immediately. Explains what consumes context: file lookups, code flow understanding, edits, test/build output, and noisy MCP JSON. Shows examples of good compaction with exact files and line numbers.

sections.title: Context Obsession: Why Context Matters
sections.summary: Explains LLMs are stateless but nondeterministic; better tokens in yield better tokens out. Every turn the agent picks from many possible next steps, and the only influence is the conversation so far. Introduces trajectory as a context optimization dimension, warning that repeatedly yelling at agents trains them to keep erring.

sections.title: The Dumb Zone Concept
sections.summary: Introduces the 'dumb zone': around 40% of the ~168k token context window, diminishing returns begin. Too many MCPs push all work into this zone. Cites Jeff Huntley's research: the more you use the context window, the worse outcomes you get.

sections.title: Sub-agents for Context Control and Research-Plan-Implement
sections.summary: Sub-agents are for controlling context, not anthropomorphizing roles—they fork out expensive reading/searching and return concise summaries. Introduces the Research-Plan-Implement workflow: research finds the right files objectively, planning outlines exact steps with code snippets and test strategies, implementation follows with low context.

sections.title: Demonstrations: BAML Rust Codebase and Parquet Java Limit
sections.summary: Demonstrates on BAML's 300k LOC Rust codebase: a oneshot fix PR accepted by the CTO, and 35,000 lines shipped in 7 hours (1-2 weeks of work). Contrasts with a failed attempt to remove Hadoop dependencies from Parquet Java, which required returning to whiteboard. Concludes: 'Do not outsource the thinking—AI can only amplify the thinking you have done or the lack of thinking you have done.'

sections.title: Semantic Diffusion and Spec-Driven Dev Critique
sections.summary: Critiques 'spec-driven dev' as suffering from semantic diffusion—Martin Fowler's 2006 observation that good terms become useless when they mean too many things to different people. The term now means everything from a detailed prompt to documentation for an open source library. Declares it overhyped and useless. Pivots to four tactical things that actually work today.

sections.title: Agent Onboarding and Progressive Disclosure
sections.summary: Uses the film Memento as analogy: agents without onboarding make things up. Recommends progressive disclosure—placing context files at each level of the repo hierarchy so agents pull only relevant context, preserving smart zone capacity. Warns that onboarding docs get out of date and contain 'lies' proportional to distance from actual code. Prefers on-demand compressed context built from code truth via sub-agents taking vertical slices through the codebase.

sections.title: Mental Alignment and Plan Review
sections.summary: Explains mental alignment as the real purpose of code review—keeping the team on the same page about how the codebase is changing. Technical leaders can read plans instead of every line of code. Cites Mitchell's practice of putting agent threads on PRs so reviewers see exact steps, prompts, and build results. Plans should include actual code snippets for leverage and reliable execution. There is a sweet spot between plan length and readability.

sections.title: Don't Outsource the Thinking: Human Review as Highest Leverage
sections.summary: Emphasizes human review of research and plans as the highest-leverage activity. A bad line of code is one bad line, but a bad plan line could be a hundred bad lines, and a bad research line derails the entire effort. Warns against tools that spew markdown to make you feel good. Context engineering effort should scale with problem complexity—simple changes need less, hard problems need more. Finding the sweet spot takes reps; pick one tool and iterate.

sections.title: RPI, Harness Engineering, and What's Next
sections.summary: Acknowledges people call the workflow RPI though the important part is compaction and staying in the smart zone, not the specific steps. Introduces 'harness engineering' as a hypy term for customizing integration points with coding tools. Predicts coding agents will be commoditized and the real challenge is adapting team workflows and culture. Describes a growing rift: staff engineers avoid AI, mid-levels produce slop, seniors resent cleanup. Cultural change must come from the top. HumanLayer is hiring to build an agentic IDE for teams to speedrun 99% AI-generated code.
